extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (attorneys/agents practicing before the USPTO)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, definitions, and sanctioning criteria used by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline and the Administrative Law Judge to evaluate alleged professional misconduct by persons practicing before the USPTO and to determine appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to suspend or exclude (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the USPTO if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO has 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' (Kroll v. Finnerty, 242 F.3d 1359, 1364 (Fed. Cir. 2001)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. The Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the standard of proof for finding violations and for evaluating affirmative defenses in USPTO disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct and dishonesty (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a)-(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Code provided that '[a] practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct' and 'shall not ... [e]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; or ... in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a broad proscription covering dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; violations may be charged under these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribed conduct includes 'Knowingly giving false or misleading information or knowingly participating in a material way in giving false or misleading information to, a client in connection with any immediate, prospective, or pending business before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to attorney-client communications about patentability, scope of claims, and representations about what a patent covers; knowingly misleading a client about matter before the USPTO violates the Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules proscribing conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)-(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The current USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct continue to proscribe conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules are the modern counterpart to the older Code provisions and are used to charge conduct that undermines adjudicative or regulatory processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dishonesty, deceit, and misrepresentation (interpretive guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of codified definitions the Court looks to common dictionary definitions: dishonesty = 'characterized by lack of truth, honesty, or trustworthiness'; deceit = 'the quality of being dishonest or misleading'; misrepresentation = 'the act of making a false or misleading assertion ... includes not just written or spoken words but also any other conduct that amounts to a false assertion.' (Merriam-Webster; Black's Law Dictionary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court uses dictionary and case-law definitions to interpret statutory/regulatory terms when not defined in the rules; misrepresentation can be by conduct, not only words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duty: communication and disclosure (37 C.F.R. § 11.104; ABA Model Rule 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner-client relationship is fiduciary; the attorney's fiduciary duty includes communication and disclosure of material information regarding the matter at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A client's signature on a declaration does not absolve the practitioner of the duty to disclose material changes and to explain material matters. Clients reasonably rely on attorneys' representations; attorneys must proactively inform clients of material changes and obtain consent where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client signature/declared review does not excuse nondisclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A client's signed declaration (e.g., 'I have reviewed and understand the contents...') does not absolve the attorney of fiduciary responsibilities or negate violations arising from nondisclosure or misrepresentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejects defenses that shift responsibility to the client for failing to detect attorney deceit; reasonable reliance on attorney is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice — definition and examples (case-law guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice is 'conduct which impedes or subverts the process of resolving disputes; it is conduct which frustrates the fair balance of interests or 'justice' essential to litigation or other proceedings.' (In re Friedman). Procuring a promise not to file a disciplinary complaint and paying clients to avoid complaints are examples of such conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines public confidence in the legal profession or impedes complaint/adjudicative processes is prejudicial and sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining appropriate sanctions, consider: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors are applied together to determine sanction severity; the decision explicitly lists and applies them in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors identified include: extensive prior disciplinary history, indifference and delay in making payments, failure to acknowledge wrongful conduct, and significant experience/knowledge of the law used to deceive or delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior discipline, repeated misconduct, knowledge/experience that makes the misconduct more blameworthy, and refusal to make restitution or acknowledge wrongdoing weigh toward more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court considers the existence of any mitigating factors (though none were found here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples implicitly include restitution, acknowledgement of wrongdoing, cooperation, absence of prior discipline; absence of mitigating factors can increase sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court often looks to the ABA's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance when determining the proper length and severity of a sanction, or when determining whether aggravating or mitigating factors exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA Standards are not dispositive but are authoritative guidance for calibrating sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential sanctions and remedial procedures (exclusion, duties, reinstatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate sanctions may include exclusion from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters. Respondent remains excluded until reinstatement is granted pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.60(c). The respondent's duties during exclusion are set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions impose concrete professional disabilities; the decision orders exclusion and references the regulatory provisions governing duties during exclusion and the reinstatement process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and procedural timelines (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of Appeal Rights: Within thirty (30) days of this initial decision, either party may appeal to the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notifies parties of the statutory/regulatory appeal window and applicable rule citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical evidentiary/interpretive approach (court will examine all issues and evidence; deem immaterial issues unaddressed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court 'has considered all issues and examined all evidence contained in the record and presented at hearing' and will deem unaddressed issues to 'lack materiality or importance to the decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court focuses analysis on material issues and relies on the evidentiary record; peripheral claims or abandoned defenses are not separately analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of misconduct fact patterns that meet the standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples applied here: making material amendments to a final draft application without client consent or disclosure; knowingly assuring a client of patentability despite prior art that precludes the claimed scope; negotiating/attempting to pay a client not to file disciplinary complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete fact patterns illustrate how regulatory prohibitions and sanctioning factors are applied to real practitioner conduct.
